Jialiang Wang, Qing Ma, Xiong Zhou, Gangfeng Hu, Haoliang Li and Xianming Liu

Internal Discrepancy for Contrastive Learning: Generalization Bounds and Downstream Behaviors

Jialiang Wangcswjl@stu.hit.edu.cn ††thanks: Equal contribution    Qing Ma11footnotemark: 1 qingma2016@gmail.com Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China    Xiong Zhoucszx.hit@gmail.com Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, China    Gangfeng Hu csgf@hit.edu.cn Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, China    Haoliang Li haoliang.li@cityu.edu.hk Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China    Xianming Liu csxm@hit.edu.cn ††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, China
Abstract

Contrastive learning has emerged as a popular paradigm for training representation models. While prior studies pursue more practical and less restrictive assumptions to enhance theoretical understanding of contrastive learning, they essentially describe the interconnections among representations within the data or induced by the function class. To encapsulate these assumptions, we propose the measure of internal discrepancy that quantifies the difference between the mean representation of positive samples and latent cluster centers. We then prove an internal discrepancy-aware generalization bound for downstream supervised tasks following contrastive learning, without requiring additional assumptions. This generalization bound not only serves as a unifying framework connecting various assumptions but also motivates us to further reduce the internal discrepancy, thereby introducing the relaxed k-means loss as an approximation. Moreover, we investigate the downstream behaviors of contrastive learning from the perspective of contrastive learning-incurred supervised losses. In the presence of class imbalance, we shed light on why contrastive learning can facilitate imbalanced learning. Finally, we investigate the optimality of these incurred supervised losses, proving several intriguing properties.

1 Introduction

In the past decade of machine learning research, many classification models have relied heavily on the availability of a large amount of labeled data (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; He et al., 2016; Vaswani et al., 2017). However, it is not always possible to obtain sufficient labeled data for scaling up models, prompting researchers to leverage vast amounts of unlabeled data (Misra and Maaten, 2020; Grill et al., 2020; Goyal et al., 2021; Tomasev et al., 2022; He et al., 2022; Kong and Zhang, 2023; Dehghani et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025), with self-supervised learning emerging as a promising path to advance machine learning (Balestriero et al., 2023). In particular, we focus on contrastive learning that captures semantically relevant and discriminative information from the data by bringing the representations of positive pairs closer together while pushing the representations of negative samples apart (Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2012; He et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2020a; Caron et al., 2021; Hieu et al., 2025; Rusak et al., 2025).

Despite the empirical success of contrastive learning (Mikolov et al., 2013; Logeswaran and Lee, 2018; Radford et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023), there remains a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding how this paradigm effectively learns meaningful representations that facilitate downstream tasks (Tian et al., 2020b; Garrido et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024; Wang, 2025). For instance, Kang et al. (2021) observed that contrastive learning can achieve a balanced representation space in the presence of class imbalance, but there has been limited theoretical analysis of this phenomenon. Due to the absence of supervision, contrastive learning primarily relies on the intrinsic structure within the data (Tian et al., 2020b; Li and Neuman, 2026), and the inductive biases of the function class and training algorithm (Wen and Li, 2021; Saunshi et al., 2022; HaoChen and Ma, 2023; Parulekar et al., 2023). However, without further assumptions on the data or inductive biases, relying solely on contrastive losses may not adequately establish relevant associations for downstream behaviors.

Prior studies have introduced various data assumptions to bridge this gap, including the (nearly) conditional independence between positive samples (Saunshi et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021; Zou and Liu, 2023), the overlap of augmentation sets for semantically similar samples (HaoChen et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022), the expansion or concentration within augmentation sets (Wei et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023), and the label consistency of positive pairs (Zhang et al., 2025). While these studies pursue more practical and less restrictive data assumptions to understand contrastive learning, Saunshi et al. (2022) pointed out that data assumptions alone, even with a small contrastive loss, are insufficient to capture the success of contrastive learning in realistic scenarios. They further argue that understanding contrastive learning requires incorporating inductive biases of the function class. This has motivated studies to investigate constrained function classes, such as assumptions regarding the ability to implement stronger inner-cluster connections (HaoChen and Ma, 2023), cluster-preserving representations (Parulekar et al., 2023), and centered representations (Cui et al., 2025). In light of these two lines of research, several critical questions arise:

  1. 1.

    Do prior data assumptions that appear distinct essentially characterize or constrain a common aspect? Is there a measure that connects these data assumptions?

  2. 2.

    Can this measure effectively describe the inductive biases of the function class or training algorithm?

  3. 3.

    Can we further establish a generalization bound based on this measure without requiring additional assumptions, thus providing a unified framework for studying both data assumptions and inductive biases?

  4. 4.

    Can we further explore the downstream behaviors of contrastive learning, including its handling of class imbalance and its optimality?

We answer these questions affirmatively. The core insight lies in the observation that prior assumptions essentially or partially describe the interconnections among representations of samples, augmentations, and latent clusters. To quantify these interconnections, we propose the measure of internal discrepancy, denoted by Disc⁡(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f), which characterizes the discrepancy between the mean representation of positive samples and latent cluster centers. Without relying on specific assumptions, we prove an internal discrepancy-aware generalization bound on downstream supervised performance for contrastive learning, expressed informally as Lsup​(f^)≲Lcon​(f)+Disc⁡(f^)+GenML_{\mathrm{sup}}(\widehat{f})\lesssim L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f})+\mathrm{Gen}_{M} for any f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}. Here, Lsup​(f^)L_{\mathrm{sup}}(\widehat{f}) is a supervised loss w.r.t. the empirical minimizer f^\widehat{f}, Lcon​(f)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f) represents the contrastive loss, and GenM\mathrm{Gen}_{M} denotes the generalization error. This bound suggests that downstream performance will be determined by both the value of the contrastive loss and the internal discrepancy. By further establishing the association between specific assumptions and the internal discrepancy, we can readily develop theoretical insights into downstream tasks with those assumptions. Replacing Disc⁡(f^)\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f}) with the intra-class discrepancy of ff and the positive-pair alignment of f^\widehat{f} in the bound motivates us to minimize an approximation of the internal discrepancy, namely the relaxed k-means loss, which aims to reduce the distance between representations within a truncated range.

Moreover, the supervised loss Lsup​(f^)L_{\mathrm{sup}}(\widehat{f}) corresponds to a specific supervised loss function, which we refer to as a contrastive learning-incurred supervised loss. Based on the incurred supervised loss, we provide insights into the downstream behaviors of contrastive learning, specifically through the InfoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018) and the spectral contrastive loss (SpeCL) (HaoChen et al., 2021). In class-imbalanced scenarios, we prove that the InfoNCE-incurred loss approximates the balanced softmax loss (Ren et al., 2020) that accommodates class distribution shifts to mitigate class imbalance, and that the cosine similarities between representations learned by the SpeCL-incurred loss remain consistent regardless of the class distribution. These results help explain why contrastive learning can facilitate class-imbalanced learning. Furthermore, we explore the optimality of these contrastive learning-incurred supervised losses, proving that representations learned under the InfoNCE-incurred loss exhibit variability collapse and converge to a simplex equiangular tight frame. Additionally, the SpeCL-incurred loss leads to optimal features that achieve the best approximation of the identity matrix.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce internal discrepancy, a measure that characterizes the discrepancy between the mean representation of positive samples and latent cluster centers and can be associated with various data assumptions.

  • •

    We derive the internal discrepancy-aware generalization bound on downstream performance for contrastive learning without requiring assumptions on the data. The generalization bound motivates us to propose the relaxed k-means loss to approximately minimize the internal discrepancy.

  • •

    We investigate the role of contrastive learning in mitigating class imbalance, revealing that the InfoNCE-incurred loss approximates the balanced softmax loss and that class imbalance only scales representations under the SpeCL-incurred loss.

  • •

    We prove the optimality of contrastive learning through its incurred supervised losses, including variability collapse and convergence to a simplex equiangular tight frame for the InfoNCE-incurred loss, and the best approximation to the identity matrix by optimal representations for the SpeCL-incurred loss.

2 Preliminaries

Notation.

Let 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} denote the set of all possible data points, 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} be the total label space, and ℱ{\mathcal{F}} be the function class of norm-bounded representation functions f:𝒳→ℝdf:{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{d} s.t. ‖f⁡(⋅)‖≤R\|f(\cdot)\|\leq R for some R>0R>0. We define 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} as the distribution of samples11 1 For ease of exposition, we consider a distribution over original samples and their augmentations., 𝒟c{\mathcal{D}}^{c} as its component w.r.t. class cc, and 𝒟𝒯{\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}} as the joint distribution of samples and their corresponding labels within the (latent) class space 𝒯⊆𝒴{\mathcal{T}}\subseteq{\mathcal{Y}}. Let ρ𝒯\rho_{\mathcal{T}} be the class distribution of 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} and |𝒯||{\mathcal{T}}| be the cardinality of 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}. Throughout, we assume |𝒯|≥2|{\mathcal{T}}|\geq 2 and ρ𝒯​(c)>0\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)>0 for all c∈𝒯c\in{\mathcal{T}}. We further assume that each sample x∼𝒟x\sim{\mathcal{D}} has a deterministic label yy, and write (x,y)∼𝒟𝒯(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}} for brevity.

Supervised Loss.

The loss incurred by the classifier g:𝒳→ℝ|𝒯|g:{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|} on a point (x,y)∼𝒟𝒯(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}} is defined as h⁡(g​(x)y,{g​(x)c}c∈𝒯,c≠y)h\left(g(x)_{y},\{g(x)_{c}\}_{c\in{\mathcal{T}},c\neq y}\right), typically tailored for enlarging the prediction g​(x)yg(x)_{y} of the target class while reducing the predictions for non-target classes {g​(x)c}c≠y\{g(x)_{c}\}_{c\neq y}. Consequently, the supervised loss w.r.t. the classifier gg is

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,g,h)=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝒯​[h⁡(g​(x)y,{g​(x)c}c∈𝒯,c≠y)].L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},g,h)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}[h(g(x)_{y},\{g(x)_{c}\}_{c\in{\mathcal{T}},c\neq y})]. (1)
Linear Probing.

To evaluate the downstream classification performance of the representation model ff, we train a linear classifier W∈ℝ|𝒯|×dW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|\times d} and use g⁡(x)=W​f​(x)g(x)=Wf(x) to calculate the classification loss Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h). By fixing ff and optimizing the linear classifier, we use a slight abuse of notation and define the supervised loss of ff on 𝒟𝒯{\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}} as the infimum over WW:

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,f,h)=infW∈ℝ|𝒯|×dLsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h).L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},f,h)=\inf_{W\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|\times d}}L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h). (2)

Since Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,f,h)≤Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},f,h)\leq L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h) for any WW, we focus on bounding a surrogate classification loss with the mean classifier that comprises class means of representations (Saunshi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Joshi and Mirzasoleiman, 2023). Throughout this paper, unless otherwise specified, WW is the mean classifier, i.e., wc=𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)w_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x) for all c∈𝒯c\in{\mathcal{T}}.

Contrastive Learning.

Contrastive learning is based on the fundamental idea of bringing representations of positive pairs closer while pushing representations of negative samples apart. We model an anchor xx and its positive sample x+x^{+} by the joint distribution 𝒟pos​(x,x+)=𝒟⁡(x)​𝒟pos​(x+|x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^{+})={\mathcal{D}}(x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x^{+}|x)22 2 In supervised contrastive learning, 𝒟pos​(x+|x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x^{+}|x) specifically includes samples that belong to the same class as xx. In the unsupervised setting, 𝒟pos​(x+|x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x^{+}|x) covers the distribution of random views (or augmentations) of xx., and k≥1k\geq 1 negative samples {xi−}i=1k\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k} are drawn i.i.d. from 𝒟neg​(x−|x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}(x^{-}|x)33 3 For supervised contrastive learning, 𝒟neg​(x−|x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}(x^{-}|x) is characterized by 𝒟y̸x​(x−){\mathcal{D}}^{\not y_{x}}(x^{-}), which represents samples from classes other than the class of xx. In the unsupervised scenario, 𝒟neg​(x−|x)=𝒟⁡(x−)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}(x^{-}|x)={\mathcal{D}}(x^{-}) describes the overarching data distribution, encompassing all classes without using label information.. The population contrastive loss is defined as

Lcon​(f,𝒟,ℓ)=𝔼x,x+∼𝒟pos{xi−}i=1k​∼i.i.d​𝒟neg​ℓ​(f,x,x+,{xi−}i=1k),L_{\mathrm{con}}(f,{\mathcal{D}};\ell)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}\end{subarray}}\ell\left(f,x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right), (3)

where ℓ\ell represents the contrastive loss function. For the sake of brevity, we will use ℓ⁡(f,x,x+,{xi−}i=1k)\ell\left(f,x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right) to denote ℓ⁡(f​(x)⊤​f​(x+),{f​(x)⊤​f​(xi−)}i=1k)\ell\left(f(x)^{\top}f(x^{+}),\{f(x)^{\top}f(x_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{k}\right). Additionally, we might abbreviate Lcon​(f,𝒟,ℓ)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f,{\mathcal{D}};\ell) as Lcon​(f,ℓ)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f;\ell) or Lcon​(f)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f) in certain contexts. Intuitively, the essence of minimizing the contrastive loss lies in amplifying the similarity between positive-pair representations f⁡(x)f(x) and f⁡(x+)f(x^{+}), while striving to separate the representations of negative samples. Correspondingly, Wang and Isola (2020) have identified two properties related to this process: the alignment of positive pairs and the uniformity of features.

We exemplify two contrastive loss functions below. The first is the widely used InfoNCE loss:

Example 1 (InfoNCE).

The InfoNCE loss in contrastive learning (Oord et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; He et al., 2020) is defined as ℓ⁡(f,x,x+,{xi−}i=1k)=log⁡[1+∑i=1kexp⁡(f​(x)⊤​(f⁡(xi−)−f⁡(x+)))]\ell(f,x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k})=\log\left[1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp(f(x)^{\top}(f(x_{i}^{-})-f(x^{+})))\right].

The second is the spectral contrastive loss that is both sample-contrastive and dimension-contrastive (HaoChen et al., 2021; HaoChen and Ma, 2023; HaoChen et al., 2022; Balestriero and LeCun, 2022; Zhou et al., 2024), acting as a well-established theoretical surrogate for the InfoNCE loss:

Example 2 (Spectral Contrastive Loss (SpeCL)).

The spectral contrastive loss (HaoChen et al., 2021) is formulated as ℓ⁡(f,x,x+,{xi−}i=1k)=−2​f​(x)⊤​f​(x+)+1k​∑i=1k(f​(x)⊤​f​(xi−))2\ell(f,x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k})=-2f(x)^{\top}f(x^{+})+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left(f(x)^{\top}f(x_{i}^{-})\right)^{2}.

As detailed in Appendix A.1, the separate convexity of the InfoNCE loss and the spectral contrastive loss can be easily verified w.r.t. the representations f⁡(x)f(x), f⁡(x+)f(x^{+}), and f⁡(xi−)f(x_{i}^{-}). Furthermore, these two loss functions are also Lipschitz continuous when ff adheres to bounded norm constraints. Therefore, we consider contrastive loss functions with both convexity and Lipschitzness.

For the tuples {(xj,xj+,{xj​i−}i=1k)}j=1M\left\{\left(x_{j},x_{j}^{+},\{x_{ji}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right)\right\}_{j=1}^{M} drawn i.i.d. according to the sampling scheme above, the empirical counterpart is defined as

L^con​(f)=1M​∑j=1Mℓ⁡(f,xj,xj+,{xj​i−}i=1k).\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{con}}(f)=\frac{1}{M}\sum\nolimits_{j=1}^{M}\ell\left(f,x_{j},x_{j}^{+},\{x_{ji}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right). (4)

The goal of contrastive learning is to identify the risk minimizer f∗∈arg​minf∈ℱ⁡Lcon​(f,𝒟)f^{*}\in\argmin_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}L_{\mathrm{con}}(f,{\mathcal{D}}). In practical scenarios, where access is limited to a finite number of samples, our focus pivots towards finding the empirical risk minimizer f^∈arg​minf∈ℱ⁡L^con​(f)\widehat{f}\in\argmin_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{con}}(f). As in supervised learning, the generalization bound for contrastive learning is measured by the difference between f^\widehat{f} and f∗f^{*}, but with a greater emphasis on bounding the downstream supervised loss Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f^,h)L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},W\widehat{f},h) for some WW.

3 Internal Discrepancy for Contrastive Learning

In this section, we begin by introducing the concept of internal discrepancy and its relationship to various assumptions outlined in the literature. Following this, we establish an internal discrepancy-aware generalization bound for contrastive learning, which does not rely on any specific data assumptions. Moreover, we propose the relaxed k-means loss as a means to approximate the minimization of internal discrepancy. Additional results for scenarios involving a single negative sample are provided in Appendix B.

3.1 Internal Discrepancy

Despite the empirical success of contrastive learning, a significant gap persists in theoretical understanding of how this paradigm effectively learns meaningful relationships between data points. Due to the absence of labels in the data, contrastive learning primarily relies on the associations within the data and their augmentations, and the inductive biases of the function class. Prior studies have presented various data assumptions to establish relevant theories, such as conditional independence of positive pairs (Saunshi et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021; Zou and Liu, 2023) and the overlap of augmentation sets (HaoChen et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). They have also considered assumptions on the function class, including centered representations (Cui et al., 2025). While diverse, these assumptions essentially or at least partially describe interconnections between samples, augmentations, and latent clusters.

To essentially measure these interconnections, we define the internal discrepancy as follows:

Definition 3 (Internal Discrepancy).

For the data distribution 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} with latent classes 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}, the internal discrepancy is defined as follows:

Disc⁡(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{Disc}(f) =𝔼c∼ρ𝒯x∼𝒟c‖𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+)−𝔼x∼𝒟cf(x)‖,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}\\ x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}\end{subarray}}\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+})-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x)\right\|, (5)

where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm.

Internal discrepancy quantitatively characterizes the alignment between the mean representation of positive samples of a data point and the classwise mean representation. Moreover, we have:

Disc⁡(f)≤\displaystyle\mathrm{Disc}(f)\leq 𝔼x,x+∼𝒟pos​(x,x+)​‖f⁡(x+)−f⁡(x)‖⏟positive-pair alignment ​Disca​(f)+𝔼c∼ρ𝒯x∼𝒟c​‖f⁡(x)−𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)‖⏟intra-class discrepancy ​Disci​(f),\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^{+})}\|f(x^{+})-f(x)\|}_{\text{positive-pair alignment }\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f)}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}\\ x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}\end{subarray}}\|f(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x)\|}_{\text{intra-class discrepancy }\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f)}, (6)

which implies that internal discrepancy is further governed by two key components: the positive-pair alignment term Disca​(f)\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f), also referred to as the alignment loss (Wang and Isola, 2020), and the intra-class discrepancy Disci​(f)\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f) that measures the discrepancy between the representations of individual samples and their respective latent class means. While prior works often posit specific assumptions that appear distinct, we demonstrate that they essentially serve as conditions to constrain the value of internal discrepancy Disc⁡(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f) or the two terms in its upper bound. Figure 1 illustrates a configuration in which more compact class clouds and local positive-pair regions accompany a smaller distance between the conditional positive mean and the class mean, reducing internal discrepancy.

Association with Previous Assumptions.

The internal discrepancy metric provides a novel perspective for integrating and expanding upon assumptions made in prior literature regarding data characteristics (Saunshi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025) and the function class (HaoChen and Ma, 2023; Parulekar et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2025):

(i) The assumption of conditional independence of positive-pair draws (Saunshi et al., 2019) states that 𝒟pos​(x,x+|c)=𝒟c​(x)​𝒟c​(x+)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^{+}|c)={\mathcal{D}}^{c}(x){\mathcal{D}}^{c}(x^{+}). This leads to a zero internal discrepancy (Disc⁡(f)=0\mathrm{Disc}(f)=0), as 𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+)=𝔼x∼𝒟cf(x)\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x).

(ii) The perfect alignment assumption between positive pairs (or the augmentation-invariant assumption) (Wang et al., 2022, Assumption 4.6) implies f⁡(x)=f⁡(x+)f(x)=f(x^{+}) for all x,x+∼𝒟pos​(x,x+)x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^{+}), that is, Disca​(f)=0\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f)=0. Moreover, the internal discrepancy Disc⁡(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f) simplifies to the intra-class discrepancy 𝔼c∼ρ𝒯x∼𝒟c​‖f⁡(x)−𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)‖\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}\\ x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}\end{subarray}}\left\|f(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x)\right\|, quantified as the expected distance between each sample and its corresponding class mean.

(iii) The (σ,δ)(\sigma,\delta)-augmentation described by Huang et al. (2023, Definition 1) means that for each class, whose sample set is GcG_{c}, there exists a subset Gc0⊆GcG_{c}^{0}\subseteq G_{c} such that ℙ[x∈Gc0]≥σℙ[x∈Gc]{\mathbb{P}}[x\in G_{c}^{0}]\geq\sigma{\mathbb{P}}[x\in G_{c}] with σ∈(0,1]\sigma\in(0,1] and supx1,x2∈Gc0dA​(x1,x2)≤δ\sup_{x_{1},x_{2}\in G_{c}^{0}}d_{A}(x_{1},x_{2})\leq\delta, where dA​(x1,x2)=minx1′∈A⁡(x1),x2′∈A⁡(x2)⁡‖x1′−x2′‖d_{A}(x_{1},x_{2})=\min_{x_{1}^{\prime}\in A(x_{1}),x_{2}^{\prime}\in A(x_{2})}\|x_{1}^{\prime}-x_{2}^{\prime}\| for augmentation AA. Under the additional assumptions of ϵ{\epsilon}-close representations among augmented data (‖f⁡(x1)−f⁡(x2)‖≤ϵ\|f(x_{1})-f(x_{2})\|\leq{\epsilon} for all x1,x2∈A⁡(x)x_{1},x_{2}\in A(x)) and ι\iota-Lipschitzness of ff in Huang et al. (2023), we obtain Disc⁡(f)≤σ2​(ι​δ+2​ϵ)+2​R​(1−σ2)\mathrm{Disc}(f)\leq\sigma^{2}(\iota\delta+2{\epsilon})+2R(1-\sigma^{2}).

(iv) The ℱ{\mathcal{F}}-implementable inner-cluster connection larger than β\beta assumption (HaoChen and Ma, 2023, Assumption 3.3) implies 𝔼x,x+∼𝒟posc​‖f⁡(x+)−f⁡(x)‖2≥β​𝔼x∼𝒟c​‖f⁡(x)−𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)‖2\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}^{c}}\|f(x^{+})-f(x)\|^{2}\geq\beta\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}\|f(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x)\|^{2} for any f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}. Then we can derive that Disc⁡(f)≤Disca​(f)+1β​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​𝔼x,x+∼𝒟posc​‖f⁡(x+)−f⁡(x)‖2\mathrm{Disc}(f)\leq\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\beta}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}^{c}}\|f(x^{+})-f(x)\|^{2}}, which measures the divergence between representations of positive pairs.

(v) For the cluster-preserving function class (Parulekar et al., 2023, Definition 4.1) satisfying f⁡(x)=f⁡(x′)f(x)=f(x^{\prime}) for all x,x′​∼i.i.d​𝒟cx,x^{\prime}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}{\mathcal{D}}^{c}, c∈𝒯c\in{\mathcal{T}} and f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}, Disc(f)=𝔼x∼𝒟∥f(x)−𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+)∥≤Disca(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\|f(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+})\|\leq\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f), which means that the internal discrepancy is bounded by the positive-pair alignment term.

(vi) For the label consistency assumption (Zhang et al., 2025, Assumption 4), positive pairs satisfy ℙx,x+∼𝒟pos[yx≠yx+]≤α{\mathbb{P}}_{x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}}[y_{x}\neq y_{x^{+}}]\leq\alpha for some α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], which yields Disc⁡(f)≤Disci​(f)+2​R​α\mathrm{Disc}(f)\leq\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f)+2R\alpha when x+x^{+} also follows the marginal distribution 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}. This implies that the internal discrepancy is bounded by the intra-class discrepancy and an additional term accounting for positive pairs from different classes. Moreover, the connected intra-class augmentation graphs and ϵ{\epsilon}-alignment conditions in Zhang et al. (2025, Assumptions 8 and 9) provide a means to control the intra-class discrepancy by propagating alignment along paths within each class.

(vii) For the centered representation assumption (Cui et al., 2025, Assumption 2.2), the original sample satisfies 𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+)=f(x)\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+})=f(x). When 𝒟c{\mathcal{D}}^{c} denotes the distribution of original samples in class cc and 𝒟pos(⋅|x)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x) is induced by augmenting the original anchor xx, we obtain Disc​(f)=Disci​(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f)=\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f) directly from the definition. This assumption constrains the mean representation of augmented samples while allowing Disca​(f)>0\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f)>0, so that the internal discrepancy reduces to the intra-class discrepancy without requiring the perfect alignment in (ii).

In essence, by formulating a generalization bound that takes into account internal discrepancy as the intermediate bridge, we can readily use specific data assumptions to develop theoretical insights into downstream tasks. This only requires us to establish the association between internal discrepancy and these data assumptions.

3.2 Internal Discrepancy-Aware Generalization Bound

We first show that there exists a supervised loss bounded by the population contrastive loss and internal discrepancy:

Theorem 4.

For the loss function ℓ\ell that is convex with respect to each of f⁡(x+)f(x^{+}) and f⁡(xi−)f(x_{i}^{-}) and η\eta-Lipschitz w.r.t. the positive representation f⁡(x+)f(x^{+}), and the distribution 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} with latent classes 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}, for all f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}, there exist a linear classifier W∈ℝ|𝒯|×dW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|\times d} and a supervised loss h:ℝ|𝒯|×𝒯→ℝh:{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|}\times{\mathcal{T}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} such that

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)≤Lcon​(f,ℓ)+η⋅Disc⁡(f),L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)\leq L_{\mathrm{con}}(f;\ell)+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(f), (7)

where equality holds if f⁡(x)=f⁡(x+)=𝔼x′∼𝒟c​f​(x′)f(x)=f(x^{+})=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x^{\prime}) for all x,x+∼𝒟poscx,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}^{c} and c∈𝒯c\in{\mathcal{T}}. And h⁡(wy⊤​f​(x),{wc⊤​f​(x)}c≠y)=𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯​ℓ​(f⁡(x),wy,{wci}i=1k)h(w_{y}^{\top}f(x),\{w_{c}^{\top}f(x)\}_{c\neq y})=\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\ell(f(x),w_{y},\{w_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k}) is the incurred supervised loss.

The following proposition shows that the internal discrepancy term in Theorem 4 cannot be dropped, even for a near-minimizer of the contrastive loss:

Proposition 5.

For any k≥1k\geq 1, class distribution ρ𝒯\rho_{\mathcal{T}}, and ϵ>0{\epsilon}>0 with d≥|𝒯|​⌈k/(2​ϵ)⌉d\geq|{\mathcal{T}}|\lceil k/(2{\epsilon})\rceil, there exist a distribution 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} with latent classes 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} and a representation ff with ‖f⁡(x)‖=R\|f(x)\|=R such that, for the InfoNCE loss with η=R\eta=R, positive samples x+=xx^{+}=x, and negative samples drawn from 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}, we have Disc⁡(f)=R\mathrm{Disc}(f)=R, the mean classifier W=0W=0, Lcon​(f)≤inff′Lcon​(f′)+ϵL_{\mathrm{con}}(f)\leq\inf_{f^{\prime}}L_{\mathrm{con}}(f^{\prime})+{\epsilon} with the infimum over all f′f^{\prime} satisfying ‖f′​(x)‖≤R\|f^{\prime}(x)\|\leq R, and

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)=log⁡(1+k)≥Lcon​(f)+η⋅Disc⁡(f)−log⁡eR2+k1+k−ϵ.L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)=\log(1+k)\geq L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(f)-\log\frac{e^{R^{2}}+k}{1+k}-{\epsilon}. (8)

Since log⁡eR2+k1+k≤eR2−11+k\log\frac{e^{R^{2}}+k}{1+k}\leq\frac{e^{R^{2}}-1}{1+k}, the bound in Theorem 4 becomes tight in this example as kk grows, with the gap Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)−Lcon​(f)L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)-L_{\mathrm{con}}(f) approaching η⋅Disc⁡(f)\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(f).

Contrastive Learning-Incurred Supervised Loss.

The supervised loss hh incurred by contrastive learning involves an expectation over kk i.i.d. class draws {ci}i=1k\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k} from ρ𝒯\rho_{\mathcal{T}} and may suffer from class collisions due to the presence of the target-class weight among the negatives. Moreover, the specific form of hh is intricately tied to factors such as the number of negatives kk and the latent class distribution ρ𝒯\rho_{\mathcal{T}}, posing practical challenges in its application. Nevertheless, the incurred loss hh can be effective for classification problems. For instance, the InfoNCE-incurred supervised loss can be reformulated as h⁡(W​f​(x),y)=∑j=0k(kj)​(ρ𝒯​(y))j​(1−ρ𝒯​(y))k−j​𝔼{ci}i=1k−j​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯y̸​log⁡[1+j+∑i=1k−jef​(x)⊤​(wci−wy)]h(Wf(x),y)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}(\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y))^{j}(1-\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y))^{k-j}\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k-j}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not y}}\log[1+j+\sum_{i=1}^{k-j}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c_{i}}-w_{y})}] (where ρ𝒯y̸\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not y} denotes the class distribution excluding class yy), which explicitly accounts for class collision. This formulation bears similarity to the cross entropy (CE) loss log⁡[1+∑c∈𝒯,c≠yef​(x)⊤​(wc−wy)]\log\left[1+\sum_{c\in{\mathcal{T}},c\neq y}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c}-w_{y})}\right]. In Figure 2 and Table 1, we demonstrate that the InfoNCE-incurred loss (we randomly sample kk classifier weights tt times) can yield comparable results to CE. Additionally, we prove below that they share the same global minimizers under mild conditions. Further analysis of the incurred loss will be developed in Section 4.

Lemma 6.

Consider the class-balanced distribution and the InfoNCE-incurred supervised risk ℋ⁡(f)=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝒯​𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯​log⁡[1+∑i=1kef​(x)⊤​(wci−wy)]{\mathcal{H}}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}}\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\log\left[1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c_{i}}-w_{y})}\right]. If d≥|𝒯|−1d\geq|{\mathcal{T}}|-1, then ℋ⁡(f){\mathcal{H}}(f) and the CE loss 𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝒯​log⁡[1+∑c≠yef​(x)⊤​(wc−wy)]\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}}\log\left[1+\sum_{c\neq y}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c}-w_{y})}\right] share the same global minimizers over all representation functions satisfying ‖f⁡(x)‖≤R\|f(x)\|\leq R.

While a variety of works have studied the capacity of contrastive learning to recover meaningful representations or latent clusters under certain data assumptions, we put forth a generalization bound for Lipschitz convex losses, which holds without any additional assumptions.

Theorem 7 (Generalization Bound).

Under the conditions in Theorem 4, assume further that ℓ\ell is η​ζ1​(R)\eta\zeta_{1}(R)-Lipschitz w.r.t. (f⁡(x),f⁡(x+),{f⁡(xi−)}i=1k)(f(x),f(x^{+}),\{f(x_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{k}) and has a range of length at most ζ2​(R)\zeta_{2}(R). With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}, there exist a linear classifier W∈ℝ|𝒯|×dW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|\times d} and a supervised loss hh such that

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f^,h)≤Lcon​(f)+η⋅Disc⁡(f^)+GenM,L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},W\widehat{f},h)\leq L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f})+\mathrm{Gen}_{M}, (9)

where GenM=O⁡(η​ζ1​(R)​ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)M+ζ2​(R)​log⁡(2/δ)M)\mathrm{Gen}_{M}=O\left(\frac{\eta\zeta_{1}(R){\mathcal{R}}_{{\mathcal{S}}}({\mathcal{F}})}{M}+\zeta_{2}(R)\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{M}}\right) and ℛ𝒮​(ℱ){\mathcal{R}}_{{\mathcal{S}}}({\mathcal{F}}) is the (unnormalized) empirical Rademacher complexity of ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on MM i.i.d. training tuples 𝒮{\mathcal{S}}.

Remark.

Theorem 7 supports the observation of Saunshi et al. (2022) that achieving a low contrastive loss alone may not guarantee good downstream performance, as exemplified by Proposition 5. A low contrastive loss and a small internal discrepancy provide sufficient control of the incurred supervised risk. This theorem also highlights several insights: (i) The inductive biases of the function class and optimization algorithm should lead to the learned model exhibiting both a low contrastive loss Lcon​(f^)L_{\mathrm{con}}(\widehat{f}) and a small internal discrepancy Disc⁡(f^)\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f}). Given that Disc⁡(f)≤Disca​(f)+Disci​(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f)\leq\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f)+\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f), improving positive-pair alignment and reducing intra-class discrepancy tighten this upper bound. (ii) In alignment with classical learning theory principles, an adequately large number MM of independent training tuples aids in reducing GenM\mathrm{Gen}_{M} when the complexity term grows sublinearly in MM. This perspective may help explain the empirical effectiveness of rich data augmentation in contrastive learning (Chen et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2023).

The incurred supervised loss further controls the classification error of the linear classifier and its balanced error that weights all classes equally:

Corollary 8.

Let hh be the InfoNCE-incurred loss in Theorem 4. For {ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}, write kc=∑i=1k𝕀⁡(ci=c)k_{c}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{I}(c_{i}=c) for c∈𝒯c\in{\mathcal{T}}, and define h0​(y)=𝔼​log⁡(1+ky)h_{0}(y)=\mathbb{E}\log(1+k_{y}) and ωk​(y)=minc≠y⁡𝔼​log⁡(1+kc1+ky)\omega_{k}(y)=\min_{c\neq y}\mathbb{E}\log\left(1+\frac{k_{c}}{1+k_{y}}\right) for y∈𝒯y\in{\mathcal{T}}. Then for any ff and WW, with any fixed rule for breaking ties, the prediction y^​(x)=arg​maxc∈𝒯⁡wc⊤​f​(x)\hat{y}(x)=\argmax_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}w_{c}^{\top}f(x) satisfies

ℙ(x,y)∼𝒟𝒯[y^(x)≠y]\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\left[\hat{y}(x)\neq y\right] ≤Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)−𝔼y∼ρ𝒯​h0​(y)miny∈𝒯⁡ωk​(y),\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}h_{0}(y)}{\min_{y\in{\mathcal{T}}}\omega_{k}(y)}, (10)
1|𝒯|∑y∈𝒯ℙx∼𝒟y[y^(x)≠y]\displaystyle\frac{1}{|{\mathcal{T}}|}\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{T}}}{\mathbb{P}}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{y}}\left[\hat{y}(x)\neq y\right] ≤Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)−𝔼y∼ρ𝒯​h0​(y)|𝒯|​miny∈𝒯​ρ𝒯​(y)​ωk​(y).\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}h_{0}(y)}{|{\mathcal{T}}|\min_{y\in{\mathcal{T}}}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y)\omega_{k}(y)}.

With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, Theorem 7 further bounds both numerators for the mean classifier of f^\widehat{f} by Lcon​(f)+R​Disc​(f^)+GenM−𝔼y∼ρ𝒯​h0​(y)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+R\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f})+\mathrm{Gen}_{M}-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}h_{0}(y) for all f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}.

Extension to Supervised Contrastive Learning.

In unsupervised contrastive learning, positive pairs usually consist of two randomly augmented views, whereas in supervised contrastive learning, positive pairs are drawn i.i.d. from the same class44 4 For the purpose of simplifying our analysis, we omit positive pairs arising from the augmentations of the same sample., embodying the principle of class-conditional independence between positive pairs (i.e., 𝒟pos​(x,x+|c)=𝒟c​(x)​𝒟c​(x+)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^{+}|c)={\mathcal{D}}^{c}(x){\mathcal{D}}^{c}(x^{+}), and Disc⁡(f)=0\mathrm{Disc}(f)=0). Consequently, all results about random negative samples presented by Saunshi et al. (2019) are relevant to the present setting.

In the supervised scenario, negative samples can instead be drawn from classes other than that of the anchor, that is, 𝒟neg​(x−|x)=𝒟y̸x​(x−)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}(x^{-}|x)={\mathcal{D}}^{\not y_{x}}(x^{-}). Then supervised contrastive learning aims at minimizing

Lconsup​(f,𝒟,ℓ)=𝔼x,x+∼𝒟pos{xi−}i=1k​∼i.i.d​𝒟neg​ℓ​(f,x,x+,{xi−}i=1k)\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{con}}^{\mathrm{sup}}(f,{\mathcal{D}};\ell)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}\end{subarray}}\ell\left(f,x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right) (11)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​𝔼x,x+​∼i.i.d​𝒟c{xi−}i=1k​∼i.i.d​𝒟c̸​ℓ​(f,x,x+,{xi−}i=1k),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,x^{+}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}{\mathcal{D}}^{c}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}{\mathcal{D}}^{\not c}\end{subarray}}\ell\left(f,x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right),

and its empirical counterpart is L^consup​(f,ℓ)\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{con}}^{\mathrm{sup}}(f;\ell). By an argument analogous to that of Theorem 7, we obtain the following result:

Theorem 9.

Under the loss conditions in Theorem 7, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}, there exist a linear classifier W∈ℝ|𝒯|×dW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|\times d} and a supervised loss h:ℝ|𝒯|×𝒯→ℝh:{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|}\times{\mathcal{T}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} such that

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f^,h)≤Lconsup​(f,𝒟,ℓ)+GenM,L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},W\widehat{f},h)\leq L_{\mathrm{con}}^{\mathrm{sup}}(f,{\mathcal{D}};\ell)+\mathrm{Gen}_{M}, (12)

where f^∈arg​minf∈ℱ⁡L^consup​(f,ℓ)\widehat{f}\in\argmin_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{con}}^{\mathrm{sup}}(f;\ell), and the incurred supervised loss is formulated as h=𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯y̸​ℓ​(f⁡(x),wy,{wci}i=1k)h=\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\not y}}\ell(f(x),w_{y},\{w_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k}).

3.3 The Relaxed K-Means Loss on Representations

As mentioned above, Theorem 4 shows that the population supervised loss is bounded by the contrastive loss Lcon​(f)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f) and the internal discrepancy Disc⁡(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f). However, the generalization bound in Theorem 7 is limited by Disc⁡(f^)\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f}), which depends on the empirical risk minimizer f^\widehat{f}. Since Disc⁡(f)≤Disca​(f)+Disci​(f)\mathrm{Disc}(f)\leq\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f)+\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f) and the positive-pair alignment Disca​(f)\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(f) is already encouraged by contrastive learning (Wang and Isola, 2020), we may also consider minimizing the empirical counterpart of the intra-class discrepancy Disci​(f)\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f):

Disc^i​(f)=1N​∑n=1N‖f⁡(xn)−μ^yxn‖,\widehat{\mathrm{Disc}}_{i}(f)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\|f(x_{n})-\widehat{\mu}_{y_{x_{n}}}\right\|, (13)

where yxny_{x_{n}} denotes the label of sample xnx_{n}, μ^c=1Nc​∑n=1Nf⁡(xn)​𝕀​(yxn=c)\widehat{\mu}_{c}=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(x_{n})\mathbb{I}(y_{x_{n}}=c), and NcN_{c} is the number of samples within class cc.

Combining Theorem 4 with a uniform bound on the estimation error of Disc^i\widehat{\mathrm{Disc}}_{i} over ℱ{\mathcal{F}}, we can derive the following proposition:

Proposition 10.

Under the notation and conditions in Theorem 7, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, any f^∈arg​minf∈ℱ⁡L^con​(f)+η⋅Disc^i​(f)\widehat{f}\in\argmin_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\cdot\widehat{\mathrm{Disc}}_{i}(f) satisfies

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f^,h)≤inff∈ℱ{Lcon​(f)+η⋅Disci​(f)}+η⋅Disca​(f^)+GenM+η⋅GenN,L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},W\widehat{f},h)\leq\inf_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}\left\{L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}_{i}(f)\right\}+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}_{a}(\widehat{f})+\mathrm{Gen}_{M}+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Gen}_{N},

where hh is the incurred supervised loss in Theorem 4, GenN=O⁡(ℛ𝒮′​(ℱ)N+R​d​|𝒯|+log⁡(2/δ)N)\mathrm{Gen}_{N}=O\left(\frac{{\mathcal{R}}_{{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}({\mathcal{F}})}{N}+R\sqrt{\frac{d|{\mathcal{T}}|+\log(2/\delta)}{N}}\right), and ℛ𝒮′​(ℱ){\mathcal{R}}_{{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}({\mathcal{F}}) is the (unnormalized) empirical Rademacher complexity of ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on 𝒮′={xn}n=1N{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}=\{x_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}.

The Relaxed K-Means Loss.

Due to the absence of specific labels for calculating Disc^i​(f)\widehat{\mathrm{Disc}}_{i}(f), we resort to using a surrogate. One intuitive approach is to employ k-means clustering to obtain CC centroids {μ^c}c∈[C]\{\hat{\mu}_{c}\}_{c\in[C]} from the representations {f⁡(xi)}i=1M\{f(x_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M}, followed by computing the minimal distance between each representation and these centroids, i.e., 1M​∑i=1Mminc∈[C]⁡‖f⁡(xi)−μ^c‖\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\min_{c\in[C]}\|f(x_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{c}\|. However, this loss is not only inefficient but also requires a predetermined number of clusters. Moreover, the uniformity property of contrastive learning and stochastic batch training would make clustering challenging and potentially imprecise. To alleviate this issue, we consider reducing the distance between representations within a certain distance range. That is, we treat each representation as a center and reduce the distance from neighboring representations to it. This can be straightforwardly implemented with a truncation as follows:

L^k​-​means​(f)=∑i,jmin⁡{‖f⁡(xi)−f⁡(xj)‖,τ},\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{k\text{-}means}}(f)=\sum_{i,j}\min\left\{\left\|f(x_{i})-f(x_{j})\right\|,\tau\right\}, (14)

where τ>0\tau>0 is a threshold to filter overly large pairwise distances. Although it requires no labels, the relaxed k-means loss controls the intra-class discrepancy as follows:

Proposition 11.

As shown in Figure 3, the incorporation of relaxed k-means loss contributes to an improvement in linear probing, especially on the ImageNet-100 dataset (the complete experimental results can be found in Appendix C.2). This underscores the feasibility of minimizing the internal discrepancy in this manner. We hope that the relaxed k-means loss can stimulate new insights into unsupervised representation learning.

4 On the Supervised Losses Incurred by Contrastive Learning

In Section 3.2, contrastive learning-incurred supervised losses are central to analyzing the downstream performance of contrastive learning. These losses entail an expectation over kk i.i.d. class draws {ci}i=1k\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k} and differ in form from typical classification losses. In this section, we investigate the behavior of the supervised losses incurred by contrastive learning, focusing specifically on InfoNCE and SpeCL.

4.1 Implications for Mitigating Class Imbalance

Real-world data often exhibits an imbalanced class distribution, primarily because some classes have an abundance of examples, while many others are associated with only a few. This class imbalance can make naive learning biased towards the majority classes, leading to poor performance and a narrow feature space for minority classes (Ren et al., 2020). However, several studies have underlined the potential of contrastive learning to improve imbalanced learning. For instance, Kang et al. (2021) observed that contrastive learning helps learn a balanced feature space, even in the presence of a highly skewed class distribution. Similarly, Li et al. (2022) argued that supervised contrastive learning can offer benefits to imbalanced learning. Nevertheless, neither study fully elucidates the underlying mechanisms driving the benefits of contrastive learning for imbalanced learning. In what follows, we theoretically demonstrate that contrastive learning implicitly mitigates class imbalance.

InfoNCE-Incurred Loss Approximates Balanced Softmax Loss.

We demonstrate that the loss incurred by InfoNCE closely approximates the balanced softmax loss (Ren et al., 2020), which accommodates class distribution shifts to mitigate class imbalance. The balanced softmax loss is expressed as h~=log⁡[𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​ef​(x)⊤​(wc−wy)]\tilde{h}=\log\left[\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c}-w_{y})}\right], where we omit the term −log⁡ρ𝒯​(y)-\log\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y) that is independent of ff and WW. We also note that the InfoNCE-incurred loss hh in Theorem 7 is defined as h⁡(x,y)=𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯​log⁡[1+∑i=1kef​(x)⊤​(wci−wy)]h(x,y)=\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\log\left[1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c_{i}}-w_{y})}\right], which can be interpreted as an approximation of log⁡[1+k​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​ef​(x)⊤​(wc−wy)]\log\left[1+k\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c}-w_{y})}\right] that resembles h~\tilde{h}. Theoretically, we confirm that

Theorem 12.

For the InfoNCE-incurred loss hh and the balanced softmax loss h~\tilde{h}, we have h=h~+log⁡k+O⁡(k−1)h=\tilde{h}+\log k+O(k^{-1}), and with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}, Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f^,h~)+log⁡k≤Lcon​(f)+η⋅Disc⁡(f^)+GenM+O⁡(k−1)L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},W\widehat{f},\tilde{h})+\log k\leq L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(\widehat{f})+\mathrm{Gen}_{M}+O(k^{-1}).

The theorem above demonstrates that the loss incurred by InfoNCE approximates the balanced softmax loss, with an error term |h−h~−log⁡k||h-\tilde{h}-\log k| that converges to zero at a rate of O⁡(k−1)O(k^{-1}). In other words, this approximation becomes progressively more accurate as the number of negatives kk increases. As shown in Figure 4 and Table 2, the performance of the InfoNCE-incurred loss usually improves for highly skewed class distributions (imbalance ratios of 50 and 100) as kk increases, which suggests that contrastive learning with more negative samples can mitigate class imbalance.

Remark.

Theorem 13 suggests that cosine similarities between features or classifier weights optimally learned by SpeCL-incurred losses remain consistent regardless of the class distribution. Hence, after projection onto the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, the nonzero optimal features and classifier weights share the same geometry as their counterparts in the class-balanced case. Moreover, we can obtain a rebalanced feature space and make balanced decisions by simply normalizing features and classifier weights within SpeCL, as guaranteed by Proposition 14 and demonstrated in Table 2.

4.2 The Optimality of Contrastive Learning-Incurred Losses

The optimal solutions of the CE loss, the MSE loss, and other losses usually exhibit neural collapse, an intriguing empirical phenomenon (Papyan et al., 2020; Mixon et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023; Wu and Mondelli, 2025), where specific manifestations in the classifier and last-layer representations are characterized. Graf et al. (2021); Jiang et al. (2024) also established neural collapse results in the empirical setting of supervised contrastive learning. Our objective here is to analyze the optimality of unsupervised or supervised contrastive learning by analyzing their incurred supervised losses.

Theorem 15 shows that the InfoNCE-incurred loss possesses an optimal structure that aligns with the structures demonstrated for CE (Papyan et al., 2020) and MSE (Zhou et al., 2022). Specifically, these representations exhibit two critical properties of neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020): (i) variability collapse, where the representations equal their class means; (ii) a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF), wherein the class means have equal length, form equal-sized angles between any given pair, and attain the maximal minimum pairwise distance.

5 Conclusion

This paper introduces the novel concept of internal discrepancy as a unifying measure for various assumptions. This measure effectively captures the relationships between representations of positive pairs and latent clusters. By establishing an internal discrepancy-aware generalization bound, we provide a bridge for understanding contrastive learning without requiring additional assumptions, while also yielding practical strategies like the relaxed k-means loss. Furthermore, we delve into the behaviors of contrastive learning-incurred supervised losses. We show that under class imbalance, the InfoNCE-incurred loss approximates the balanced softmax loss, while features learned by the SpeCL-incurred loss maintain consistent cosine similarities regardless of class distributions. This helps explain why contrastive learning can mitigate class imbalance. The optimality of contrastive learning-incurred losses also involves some intriguing properties, including neural collapse properties for InfoNCE and the best approximation to the identity matrix for SpeCL. These results not only enhance our understanding of contrastive learning but also pave the way for exploring downstream behaviors.

Appendix: Internal Discrepancy for Contrastive Learning

Appendix A Proofs of Theorems, Lemmas and Propositions

A.1 The Convexity and Lipschitzness of the InfoNCE Loss and Spectral Contrastive Loss

For fixed remaining representations, the InfoNCE loss is a log-sum-exp of affine functions, and the spectral contrastive loss is a linear function plus nonnegative quadratic terms. Thus both losses are separately convex in each representation. Their Lipschitz constants with respect to the positive representation can be taken as η=R\eta=R and η=2​R\eta=2R, respectively, by differentiating with respect to that representation.

The nonzero blocks in row ii of the Jacobian JJ are v+−vi−v^{+}-v_{i}^{-}, vv, and −v-v, corresponding to vv, v+v^{+}, and vi−v_{i}^{-}. Hence

‖J‖22≤‖J‖F2=∑i=1k(‖v+−vi−‖22+2​‖v‖22)≤6​k​R2.\|J\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|J\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigl(\|v^{+}-v_{i}^{-}\|_{2}^{2}+2\|v\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)\leq 6kR^{2}.

Proof.

The key idea in the proof is the use of the Lipschitzness of the loss function ℓ\ell and Jensen’s inequality based on the convexity of ℓ\ell with respect to f⁡(x+)f(x^{+}) and f⁡(xi−)f(x_{i}^{-}). Let μc=𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)\mu_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x) be the mean representation of the class c∈𝒯c\in{\mathcal{T}} and μyx\mu_{y_{x}} denote the mean representation of the class of the sample xx. =\displaystyle= 𝔼x∼𝒟𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)𝔼{xi−}i=1k​∼i.i.d​𝒟ℓ(f(x),f(x+),{f(xi−)}i=1k)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}\mathbb{E}_{\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}{\mathcal{D}}}\ell\left(f(x),f(x^{+}),\{f(x_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{k}\right)
≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼x∼𝒟𝔼{xi−}i=1k​∼i.i.d​𝒟ℓ(f(x),𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+),{f(xi−)}i=1k)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}{\mathcal{D}}}\ell\left(f(x),\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+}),\{f(x_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{k}\right)
≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼x∼𝒟𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯ℓ(f(x),μyx+𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+)−μyx,{μci}i=1k)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\ell\left(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}}+\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+})-\mu_{y_{x}},\{\mu_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right)
≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼x∼𝒟​𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯​ℓ​(f⁡(x),μyx,{μci}i=1k)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\ell\left(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}},\{\mu_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right)
−η⋅𝔼x∼𝒟‖𝔼x+∼𝒟pos(⋅|x)f(x+)−μyx‖\displaystyle-\eta\cdot\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}(\cdot|x)}f(x^{+})-\mu_{y_{x}}\right\|
=\displaystyle= 𝔼x∼𝒟​h​(μyx⊤​f​(x),{μc⊤​f​(x)}c≠yx,c∈𝒯)−η⋅Disc⁡(f),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}h\left(\mu_{y_{x}}^{\top}f(x),\{\mu_{c}^{\top}f(x)\}_{c\not=y_{x},c\in{\mathcal{T}}}\right)-\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(f),

where W=(μc)c∈𝒯⊤W=(\mu_{c})_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}^{\top} and h⁡(μyx⊤​f​(x),{μc⊤​f​(x)}c≠yx,c∈𝒯)=𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯​ℓ​(f⁡(x),μyx,{μci}i=1k)h\left(\mu_{y_{x}}^{\top}f(x),\{\mu_{c}^{\top}f(x)\}_{c\not=y_{x},c\in{\mathcal{T}}}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\ell\left(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}},\{\mu_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k}\right). A.2.3 Proof of Lemma 6

Proof.

Write C=|𝒯|C=|{\mathcal{T}}|, μc=𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)\mu_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x), μ¯=C−1​∑cμc\bar{\mu}=C^{-1}\sum_{c}\mu_{c}, and Δ=C−1​∑c‖μc‖2−‖μ¯‖2≤R2\Delta=C^{-1}\sum_{c}\|\mu_{c}\|^{2}-\|\bar{\mu}\|^{2}\leq R^{2}. Define

Φ⁡(z)=∑j=0k(kj)​C−j​(1−C−1)k−j​log⁡[1+j+(k−j)​ez].\Phi(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}C^{-j}(1-C^{-1})^{k-j}\log[1+j+(k-j)e^{z}].

Conditioning on the number of negative classes equal to the target class, and applying Jensen’s inequality to the other negative classes, the anchor, and the target class, gives

ℋ⁡(f)≥Φ⁡(−C​ΔC−1)≥Φ⁡(−C​R2C−1).{\mathcal{H}}(f)\geq\Phi\left(-\frac{C\Delta}{C-1}\right)\geq\Phi\left(-\frac{CR^{2}}{C-1}\right).

Every class-constant representation whose class means form a simplex ETF of radius RR attains this bound, and such representations exist since their Gram matrix C​R2C−1​(𝑰−1C​𝟏𝟏⊤)\frac{CR^{2}}{C-1}({\bm{I}}-\frac{1}{C}{\bm{1}}{\bm{1}}^{\top}) is positive semidefinite of rank C−1≤dC-1\leq d. Since Φ\Phi is strictly increasing, every global minimizer has Δ=R2\Delta=R^{2}, hence μ¯=0\bar{\mu}=0 and ‖μc‖=R\|\mu_{c}\|=R for every cc. Moreover, 𝔼x∼𝒟c​‖f⁡(x)−μc‖2=𝔼x∼𝒟c​‖f⁡(x)‖2−‖μc‖2≤R2−‖μc‖2=0\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}\|f(x)-\mu_{c}\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}\|f(x)\|^{2}-\|\mu_{c}\|^{2}\leq R^{2}-\|\mu_{c}\|^{2}=0, so f⁡(x)=μcf(x)=\mu_{c} almost surely. The event with exactly k−1k-1 negatives in the target class has positive probability. Equality in its strictly convex scalar Jensen step implies that μc⊤​μc′\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}} is constant over c′≠cc^{\prime}\neq c. As μ¯=0\bar{\mu}=0, this constant is −R2/(C−1)-R^{2}/(C-1). Hence ff minimizes ℋ⁡(f){\mathcal{H}}(f) if and only if f⁡(x)=μyxf(x)=\mu_{y_{x}} almost surely, where ‖μc‖=R\|\mu_{c}\|=R and μc⊤μc′=−R2/(C−1)\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}}=-R^{2}/(C-1) for c≠c′c\neq c^{\prime}.

Applying Jensen’s inequality in the same way to the CE risk gives

𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟𝒯​log⁡[1+∑c≠yef​(x)⊤​(μc−μy)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}}\log\left[1+\sum_{c\neq y}e^{f(x)^{\top}(\mu_{c}-\mu_{y})}\right]
≥log[1+(C−1)e−CΔ/(C−1)]≥log[1+(C−1)e−CR2/(C−1)].\displaystyle\geq\log\left[1+(C-1)e^{-C\Delta/(C-1)}\right]\geq\log\left[1+(C-1)e^{-CR^{2}/(C-1)}\right].

Every minimizer characterized above attains this bound over the same mean-classifier representations. Conversely, equality in this chain requires Δ=R2\Delta=R^{2}, which again implies μ¯=0\bar{\mu}=0, ‖μc‖=R\|\mu_{c}\|=R, and f⁡(x)=μcf(x)=\mu_{c} almost surely. Equality in the strictly convex Jensen step over c≠yc\neq y then implies that μy⊤​μc\mu_{y}^{\top}\mu_{c} is constant over c≠yc\neq y, so every minimizer of the CE risk is also a minimizer of ℋ⁡(f){\mathcal{H}}(f), completing the proof. ∎

≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼x∼𝒟​log⁡[1+k​exp⁡(f​(x)⊤​(CC−1​μ¯−CC−1​μyx))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\log\left[1+k\exp\left(f(x)^{\top}\left(\tfrac{C}{C-1}\overline{\mu}-\tfrac{C}{C-1}\mu_{y_{x}}\right)\right)\right]
≥\displaystyle\geq 1C​∑c∈𝒯log⁡[1+k​exp⁡(CC−1​μc⊤​(μ¯−μc))]\displaystyle\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}\log\left[1+k\exp\left(\tfrac{C}{C-1}\mu_{c}^{\top}(\overline{\mu}-\mu_{c})\right)\right]
≥\displaystyle\geq log⁡[1+k​exp⁡(1C−1​∑c∈𝒯μc⊤​(μ¯−μc))]\displaystyle\log\left[1+k\exp\left(\tfrac{1}{C-1}\sum_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}\mu_{c}^{\top}(\overline{\mu}-\mu_{c})\right)\right]
≥\displaystyle\geq log⁡[1+k​exp⁡(−C​R2C−1)].\displaystyle\log\left[1+k\exp\left(-\tfrac{CR^{2}}{C-1}\right)\right].

As in the proof of Lemma 6, equality in the last inequality requires μ¯=0\overline{\mu}=0 and ‖μc‖=R\|\mu_{c}\|=R, which imply f⁡(x)=μcf(x)=\mu_{c} almost surely under 𝒟c{\mathcal{D}}^{c}. The function (z1,…,zk)↦log⁡(1+∑iezi)(z_{1},\ldots,z_{k})\mapsto\log(1+\sum_{i}e^{z_{i}}) is strictly convex, so equality in the first inequality requires μc⊤​μc′\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}} to be constant over c′≠cc^{\prime}\neq c. Their sum is −R2-R^{2}, hence each equals −R2/(C−1)-R^{2}/(C-1). Conversely, the feasible simplex Gram matrix in the proof of Lemma 6 attains equality throughout, completing the proof. ∎

Theorem 23.

Consider the supervised spectral loss Lsup=𝔼x∼𝒟​𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯y̸x​ℓ​(f⁡(x),μyx,{μci}i=1k)L_{\mathrm{sup}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not y_{x}}}\ell(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}},\{\mu_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k}), that is, ℓ⁡(f⁡(x),μyx,{μci}i=1k)=−2​f​(x)⊤​μyx+1k​∑i=1k(f​(x)⊤​μci)2\ell(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}},\{\mu_{c_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{k})=-2f(x)^{\top}\mu_{y_{x}}+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}(f(x)^{\top}\mu_{c_{i}})^{2}. Then ff minimizes LsupL_{\mathrm{sup}} over all representation functions satisfying ‖f⁡(x)‖≤R\|f(x)\|\leq R if and only if f⁡(x)=μyx∗f(x)=\mu_{y_{x}}^{*} almost surely, where {μc∗}c∈𝒯\{\mu_{c}^{*}\}_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}} minimizes 𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​[−2​μc⊤​μc+𝔼c′∼ρ𝒯c̸​(μc⊤​μc′)2]\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\left[-2\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c}+\mathbb{E}_{c^{\prime}\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not c}}(\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}})^{2}\right] subject to ‖μc‖≤R\|\mu_{c}\|\leq R.

Proof.

For the spectral contrastive loss, we have

Lsup=\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{sup}}= 𝔼x∼𝒟​𝔼{ci}i=1k​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯y̸x​[−2​f​(x)⊤​μyx+1k​∑i=1k(f​(x)⊤​μci)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not{y_{x}}}}\left[-2f(x)^{\top}\mu_{y_{x}}+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}(f(x)^{\top}\mu_{c_{i}})^{2}\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼x∼𝒟​[−2​f​(x)⊤​μyx+𝔼c∼ρ𝒯y̸x​(f​(x)⊤​μc)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\left[-2f(x)^{\top}\mu_{y_{x}}+\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not{y_{x}}}}(f(x)^{\top}\mu_{c})^{2}\right]
≥\displaystyle\geq 𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​[−2​μc⊤​μc+𝔼c′∼ρ𝒯c̸​(μc⊤​μc′)2].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\left[-2\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c}+\mathbb{E}_{c^{\prime}\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not c}}(\mu_{c}^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}})^{2}\right].

Denote the last expression by Q⁡({μc})Q(\{\mu_{c}\}). It has a minimizer on the compact set ‖μc‖≤R\|\mu_{c}\|\leq R, and the corresponding class-constant representations attain the lower bound. Moreover,

Lsup−Q⁡({μc})=𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​𝔼x∼𝒟c​𝔼c′∼ρ𝒯c̸​[((f⁡(x)−μc)⊤​μc′)2].L_{\mathrm{sup}}-Q(\{\mu_{c}\})=\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}\mathbb{E}_{c^{\prime}\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not c}}\left[((f(x)-\mu_{c})^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}})^{2}\right].

Any minimizer must therefore minimize QQ and satisfy (f⁡(x)−μc)⊤​μc′=0(f(x)-\mu_{c})^{\top}\mu_{c^{\prime}}=0 almost surely for every c′≠cc^{\prime}\neq c. If a class has nonzero within-class variance, then ‖μc‖<R\|\mu_{c}\|<R and there exists a nonzero vv orthogonal to all μc′\mu_{c^{\prime}}, c′≠cc^{\prime}\neq c. Replacing μc\mu_{c} by μc+s​v\mu_{c}+sv for sufficiently small ss preserves feasibility and all cross-class inner products. Choosing the sign of ss so that 2​s​μc⊤​v+s2​‖v‖2>02s\mu_{c}^{\top}v+s^{2}\|v\|^{2}>0 strictly decreases QQ through its term −2​ρ𝒯​(c)​‖μc‖2-2\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)\|\mu_{c}\|^{2}, a contradiction. Thus every minimizer is class-constant almost surely, proving both directions. ∎

Appendix B One Negative Sample Case

To better understand the supervised loss incurred by contrastive learning, we also explore the special case where only one negative sample is used (i.e., k=1k=1). Negative sampling is also used in Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013). Here, we consider the contrastive objective with one negative sample, defined as follows:

Lcon​(f,𝒟,ℓ)=𝔼x,x+∼𝒟posx−∼𝒟neg​ℓ​(f⁡(x),f⁡(x+),f⁡(x−)).L_{\mathrm{con}}(f,{\mathcal{D}};\ell)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,x^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pos}}\\ x^{-}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{neg}}\end{subarray}}\ell(f(x),f(x^{+}),f(x^{-})). (29)

In this case, the incurred loss hh in Theorem 4 can be precisely characterized when class collision results in a constant loss value. Let π=𝔼c,c′​∼i.i.d​ρ𝒯​𝕀​(c=c′)\pi=\mathbb{E}_{c,c^{\prime}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\mathbb{I}(c=c^{\prime}). For losses satisfying ℓ⁡(v,u,u)=ℓ⁡(0)\ell(v,u,u)=\ell(0) for all ‖v‖,‖u‖≤R\|v\|,\|u\|\leq R, where ℓ⁡(0)\ell(0) is constant, we can derive a similar bound to that of Saunshi et al. (2019) without relying on the assumption of conditional independence of positive pairs.

Proposition 24.

Under the notation and conditions in Theorem 4, suppose k=1k=1 and ℓ⁡(v,u,u)=ℓ⁡(0)\ell(v,u,u)=\ell(0) is constant for ‖v‖,‖u‖≤R\|v\|,\|u\|\leq R. Then, for all f∈ℱf\in{\mathcal{F}}, there exist a linear classifier W∈ℝ|𝒯|×dW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{T}}|\times d} and a supervised loss hh such that

Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)≤Lcon​(f)+η⋅Disc⁡(f)−π⋅ℓ⁡(0),L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)\leq L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\cdot\mathrm{Disc}(f)-\pi\cdot\ell(0), (30)

where the incurred loss h⁡(wy⊤​f​(x),{wc⊤​f​(x)}c≠y)=(1−ρ𝒯​(y))​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯y̸​ℓ​(f⁡(x),wy,wc)h(w_{y}^{\top}f(x),\{w_{c}^{\top}f(x)\}_{c\neq y})=(1-\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y))\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not y}}\ell(f(x),w_{y},w_{c}).

Proof.

Let wc=μc=𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)w_{c}=\mu_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x). Splitting the mean-classifier loss according to whether the negative class equals the anchor class gives

𝔼x∼𝒟​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯​ℓ​(f⁡(x),μyx,μc)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\ell(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}},\mu_{c}) =𝔼x∼𝒟​[(1−ρ𝒯​(yx))​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯y̸x​ℓ​(f⁡(x),μyx,μc)+ρ𝒯​(yx)​ℓ​(0)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\left[(1-\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y_{x}))\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not y_{x}}}\ell(f(x),\mu_{y_{x}},\mu_{c})+\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y_{x})\ell(0)\right]
=Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)+π​ℓ​(0).\displaystyle=L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)+\pi\ell(0).

Theorem 4 bounds the left-hand side by Lcon​(f)+η​Disc​(f)L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\mathrm{Disc}(f), completing the proof. ∎

Multi-Class Binary Cross Entropy. For the InfoNCE loss with only one negative sample, we have the incurred loss

h⁡(W​f​(x),y)=(1−ρ𝒯​(y))​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯y̸​log⁡[1+ef​(x)⊤​(wc−wy)],h(Wf(x),y)=(1-\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(y))\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}^{\not y}}\log\left[1+e^{f(x)^{\top}(w_{c}-w_{y})}\right], (31)

which can be viewed as a multi-class binary cross entropy that trains the binary classifiers {wy−wc}c≠y\{w_{y}-w_{c}\}_{c\neq y} with weighted logistic losses for each sample xx drawn from 𝒟y{\mathcal{D}}^{y}.

Taking ℓ⁡(0)=log⁡2\ell(0)=\log 2 in Proposition 24 gives the deterministic InfoNCE bound Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h)≤Lcon​(f)+η​Disc​(f)−π​log⁡2L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{{\mathcal{T}}},Wf,h)\leq L_{\mathrm{con}}(f)+\eta\mathrm{Disc}(f)-\pi\log 2 for the loss in Equation 31.

For a direct classification guarantee, let h1h_{1} denote the k=1k=1 InfoNCE-incurred loss in Theorem 4, including target-class negatives, and set pmin=minc∈𝒯⁡ρ𝒯​(c)>0p_{\min}=\min_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)>0. With any fixed rule for breaking ties, the classification error under 𝒟𝒯{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{T}} satisfies

ℙ(x,y)∼𝒟𝒯[arg​maxc∈𝒯wc⊤f(x)≠y]≤Lsup​(𝒟𝒯,W​f,h1)−π​log⁡2pmin​log⁡2.{\mathbb{P}}_{(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{T}}}\left[\argmax_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}w_{c}^{\top}f(x)\neq y\right]\leq\frac{L_{\mathrm{sup}}({\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{T}},Wf,h_{1})-\pi\log 2}{p_{\min}\log 2}. (32)

This is the case k=1k=1 of the first bound in Corollary 8, since then 𝔼y∼ρ𝒯​h0​(y)=π​log⁡2\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}h_{0}(y)=\pi\log 2 and ω1​(y)=log⁡2⋅minc≠y⁡ρ𝒯​(c)≥pmin​log⁡2\omega_{1}(y)=\log 2\cdot\min_{c\neq y}\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)\geq p_{\min}\log 2, and that corollary also bounds its numerator for the mean classifier of f^\widehat{f}.

Appendix C Experiments

C.1 Experimental Details

In this section, we present the training details and experimental results across various tasks, encompassing unsupervised contrastive learning and supervised learning on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 (Krizhevsky, 2009), and ImageNet-100 (the first 100 classes of ImageNet) (Deng et al., 2009). The chosen network architectures are ResNet-18 (He et al., 2016) for CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, and ResNet-50 for ImageNet-100. All models are trained for 200 epochs using the SGD optimizer and a cosine decay learning rate schedule, with an initial learning rate of 0.2, a batch size of 512, and a weight decay of 5e-4.

C.2 More Experimental Results

More Results on the Relaxed K-Means Loss.

We conduct experiments with independent runs and report standard deviations to illustrate the performance of the relaxed k-means loss. For Table 3, we run 3 trials with random seeds (0, 1, 2) for each λ∈{0,0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5,1}\lambda\in\{0,0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5,1\}. As is evident in the table, the performance in linear probing deteriorates when λ\lambda is too large, suggesting inherent limitations of the relaxed k-means loss. This could be attributed to the fact that it only focuses on reducing distances between representations within a specific range rather than rigorously shrinking the distance to cluster centers. Consequently, this relaxation would inevitably cause representations of semantically inconsistent samples to become close, particularly in the early stage of training. Despite these limitations, we still observe an improvement, particularly on ImageNet-100.

C.3 Validation of Theorem 13

In the proof of Theorem 13, a global minimizer is obtained by minimizing ∥(ρ𝒯​(c)​μc)c∈𝒯⊤​(ρ𝒯​(c)​wc)c∈𝒯−𝑰∥F2\lVert(\sqrt{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}\mu_{c})^{\top}_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}(\sqrt{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}w_{c})_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}-{\bm{I}}\rVert_{F}^{2} over class means and classifier weights, where μc=𝔼x∼𝒟c​f​(x)\mu_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim{\mathcal{D}}^{c}}f(x). For s>0s>0, let μ^c=s​|𝒯|​ρ𝒯​(c)​μc\hat{\mu}_{c}=s\sqrt{|{\mathcal{T}}|\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}\mu_{c} and w^c=1s​|𝒯|​ρ𝒯​(c)​wc\hat{w}_{c}=\frac{1}{s}\sqrt{|{\mathcal{T}}|\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}w_{c}. The matrix objective then equals ∥(1|𝒯|​μ^c)c∈𝒯⊤​(1|𝒯|​w^c)c∈𝒯−𝑰∥F2\lVert(\frac{1}{\sqrt{|{\mathcal{T}}|}}\hat{\mu}_{c})^{\top}_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{|{\mathcal{T}}|}}\hat{w}_{c})_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}-{\bm{I}}\rVert_{F}^{2} for the class-balanced case. Both distributions attain the same minimum, so this scaling maps corresponding global minimizers while preserving cosine similarities between their nonzero features and classifier weights.

To illustrate this point, we conduct experiments on long-tailed CIFAR-10 using ResNet-18 with a feature dimension of 512, and |𝒯|=10|{\mathcal{T}}|=10. Since d≥|𝒯|d\geq|{\mathcal{T}}|, we can derive that the global minimizer of ∥(ρ𝒯​(c)​μc)c∈𝒯⊤​(ρ𝒯​(c)​wc)c∈𝒯−𝑰∥F2\lVert(\sqrt{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}\mu_{c})^{\top}_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}(\sqrt{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}w_{c})_{c\in{\mathcal{T}}}-{\bm{I}}\rVert_{F}^{2} satisfies μc⊤​wc=1ρ𝒯​(c)\mu_{c}^{\top}w_{c}=\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)}, μc⊤​wc′=0\mu_{c}^{\top}w_{c^{\prime}}=0 for c≠c′c\neq c^{\prime}. The results are presented in Table 4. As observed, the logits μc⊤​wc\mu_{c}^{\top}w_{c} of the representation model roughly align with 1ρ𝒯​(c)\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c)} across the board.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
